title: How do you structure your AI game development workflow without burning through usage limits?
author: Long-Assistance-5585
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I have a ChatGPT Plus subscription and recently started getting into AI-assisted game development. I've built apps before, but game development is new territory for me.

I'm currently experimenting with Godot and using Codex (Astra) to handle most of the coding, since I don't have much programming experience. However, I feel like I'm missing a solid foundation and a proper workflow.

My biggest problem is that I burn through my usage limits pretty quickly, especially when working on more complex tasks or going back and forth fixing bugs.

I'd love to hear how you guys approach AI game development, particularly if you're a solo developer or don't have a traditional programming background.

A few questions:

1. What's your workflow? How do you go from an initial game idea to a playable prototype using AI?
2. Which AI tools do you use? Do you combine different models or agents for coding, planning, debugging and asset creation?
3. How do you manage usage limits? Do you delegate simpler tasks to free or cheaper models and save more capable models for complex work?
4. How do you maintain consistency? How do you prevent AI from breaking existing features or losing track of your project as it grows?
5. What would you do differently if you were starting over? Are there any tools, skills, workflows or resources you'd recommend learning early?

I'm not trying to build a massive game right away. My goal is to develop small, polished games while gradually building a reliable AI-assisted development workflow.

I'd especially appreciate hearing about actual setups you're using rather than just general advice.

Thanks in advance!How do you structure your AI game development workflow without burning through usage limits?

replies.author: Den_er_da_hvid
replies.body:
Oh, to answer your questions  
1. I dont have a fixed workflow yet. But for my current game, I spend some time thinking about what the game is, and writing the first prompt took a while. Opus 5.5 is miles better than what I got with Opus 5, so that helps.  I then spend some time test-playing and changing stuff before I shared it on itch so I can get feedback. It is just a simple html game to get the feel of it.  
I then started the "real" development, in Löve2d and using inkscape for art. Again. I have a implementation plan, so I know what to spend tokens on in the comming sessions, but most of my changes is still comming from playing the game and se where stuff is off or things I think is needed.   
I just finished a session where I decided the color palette and claude gave me an artifact where I can see the old/new style compared. Giving my own color palette is better than the default ones the AI comes with. Next session is implementing new colors.  
2. Only use Claude Opus. Inkscape is nice to make and tweek art.  
Not sure what I will do with sound and music. Propably find music online.  
3. I turn the effort up and down based on how complex I think it will be.  
4. It is difficult. my prevous game I tried to make with opus 5 was difficult to manage. the output language was also difficult to understand what it ment. A lot has happened with Opus 5.5.   
5. in general, I aim for games with a smaller scope.

comments.author: JWalter89
comments.body:
You should try straight up asking Codex what is using the most tokens and how can you optimize it better for token efficiency.

I found I was having the same problem with Claude. I thought I was being really clever by having a massive amount of documentation to stop AI hallucinations, but it turned out I was using 200k tokens at the start of every session (including using subagents) and then making it use another 100k at the end of every session reconciling documentation. So Claude went through and consolidated loads of docs. And also purged loads of insanely verbose commentary in the codebase, and it went from 200k to 50k which had a massive impact on my token usage. Second week in a row now that I am nowhere near hitting my limit.

Edit: also converting regular pieces of work you ask it to do into skills that are strictly defined makes a big difference too.

comments.author: KronisLV
comments.body:
Regular Codex with their 200 USD tier, using Astra on High, plus the Blender MCP and scripting. Right now Opus 5.5 would be more economical for the use case, its 3D capabilities are somewhat better.

Engine choice probably matters a lot, I'm doing development with Flax (source available engine) and it's a joy to work with, alongside me being able to build customized versions of the engine (e.g. changing how shadow cascades are refreshed) and also reference the actual source code when questions arise.

Godot is more complex (due to the engine internals needing to support both GDScript and C# for scripting) and something like Unity doesn't even expose the source code, so the agent will need to read more docs and experiment to prove/disprove assumptions, though they are well represented in the training data and they do have a good CLI. I also looked at Stride which is all C# which is great, except it didn't have terrain support out of the box which Flax did.

Other than that, it's common sense like AGENTS.md with sub-files detailing how to work with specific things, a lot of scripts to automate common stuff, your own tools to query scene files etc., I even have validations that check that for example tree mesh LOD levels and impostors don't lose too much coverage, so if I ask AI to do 3D work it's harder for it to mess up.

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
First thing i tried was using grok to write prompts for local models to write the code. That failed. Grok ended up rewriting alot of it and it didn’t work well when it had to do engine specific stuff cuz there is alot less godot out there than like python or c# to train the model on, at least that was groks explanation.

Ok, stuff that worked. I started using obsidian notes to as much preproduction planning as possible, put the vault in the game folder so grok can see it and check my prompt against my overall vision. 

Then when i don’t have alot of tokens, i can start just sketching out major passes for next week when i do. So the first day my tokens refresh, i can use like 50/60% of the tokens on the first day but it’s catching up on all the work i decided on last week. That would be inefficient if this was my job, but it’s a hobby so it works well. 

Playtesting: i try to get to playtesting as soon as possible. Then when i playtest, i write a long list of everything i don’t like, i only stop the playtest if there is a game breaking bug. The long list is better because you can ask grok to group the items together so it doesn’t have to reference tbe entire game tk fix 4 ui issues and it doesn’t habe to pull the ui4 times. 

A major game changer for me was that grok build as access to game directory. When i was trying to copy and paste scripts in, nightmare. Doubling up on variables and functions, etc. it still does it some on grok build but alot better.

Once ive implemented five or six things, i ask it to do code review and look for refactoring. Because it builds what you ask it to build, sometimes those things will be really close and could really just be the same thing l. 

Another thing i did is i orginally did everything in godot, but for my game, i actually like unity better. Ive used unity alot more doing game jams and whatnot and i can tell it, put all these variables in the same script so i can tweak balance in one place in the inspector. I’m sure u can do that in godot as well i’m just not as familar with it and didn’t want to learn how. 

What i’m trying next is grok build, local scale, grok review. If i make a class of like magic sword or something and now i need 50 magic swords, my local  
can fill out those fields. I never give the local acess to actual game files cuz i did once and basically they argued about code and deleted a bunch of stuff. Not ideal but ive known engineers so i wasn’t suprised.

replies.author: 0bscuris
replies.body:
I don’t know how much difference there is between the enterprise models, i suspect little or that the differences are under the hood and i won’t understand them. 

There is a clear difference between a local 30b model and an enterprise model, but i suspect it’s sorta like comparing cars. If you take a 25k car and a 50k car they r different but if you take a 50k car and another 50k car they r close. 

But i don’t think the car matters as much as people think it does. How you drive matters more. Good prompters who can clearly articulate what they r looking for without biasing the model, are better drivers and they get more out of the engine for same amount of gas.

comments.author: ManyObras
comments.body:
El workflow lo suelo crear yo mismo con aplicaciones de paneles como Trello. Apunto las ideas que se me ocurren, les doy prioridad y lo "gamifico" creando tareas dentro de esas ideas. También suelo usar las tablas de Hojas de calculo de Google que permiten mucha personalización. No hace falta que estés mucho tiempo, solo para leerlo a tu gusto y tener un acceso cómodo a la información.
Por otro lado, lo que si hago con modelos de lenguaje (ahora mismo uso Claude Opus) son documentos de plan de desarrollo y de sistemas ya implementados. Le doy instrucciones de forma que escriba un documento en Markdown (archivo .md) de forma que yo lo pueda leer fácil y el modelo pueda leerlo y entender el contexto, así como otros sistemas a los que va ligado.
Por ejemplo: quieres crear un sistema de inventario. Le das las características que quieres y como quieres que se comporte con el resto de sistemas > Con esto creas el plan de desarrollo y lo dejas guardado en la carpeta > La IA seguirá estos pasos para desarrollar > Cuando acabes de desarrollar este sistema, documentas lo que has hecho y lo dejas guardado. En el futuro el modelo de lenguaje solo tiene que leer ese archivo para entender su arquitectura y construir sobre el. 
Crear este tipo de archivos no consume demasiados tokens y te permite tener el proyecto controlado en todo momento.

comments.author: ZymzAlchemy
comments.body:
I spent the time to build a standardized template I use for every game. It has all the common core items most games will require, to prevent rewriting code, wasting usage, and possibly introducing new bugs when it's easier to reuse code that's already been tested, is rock solid, and ready to go. (This does 40% of your work for you before you begin and exports to Windows/Linux/Android/Web).

Every game starts with a concept, a roadmap (What do I want the end product to look like, play like, feel like, this includes writing a concept document (markdown) and generating several concept 'screenshots' of what the game's final look will be, give or take. all of these are built with the template in mind, the template is the governing core and all architecture is built on that existing core.

Once I've written a roadmap I creat a phased architectural blueprint in phases. Each phases is it's own markdown file which is an isolated task I want the agent to perform. It instructs the agent to begin reading the 'AGENTS.md' and the phasing document for the current phase while also instructing it to remain within this scope. I outline the task, the files I want created, the method and loctions I want them created in, and write the rudimentary functions/code snippets needed to demonstrate the task I want performed.

Once I have all of the, placed into a projet folder in the locations I write a meticulous 'AGENTS.md' file that gives the agent guardrails. This is what I want you to do, this is what I do not want you to do. If you have ambiguous scenarios or obstructions you cannot resolve without bending/breaking the established rules or the project, stop and notify me (the operator) and I will review the task/context and provide remediation instructions (never invent code/functions/make architectural deviation decisions without operator approval). 

Every phase ends with a sub-agent dispatched to verify the previous agent performed the work it claims it performed. Performed this work accurately. Performed the appropriate test available or created the new harness for the phase as requested and performed these tests. Wrote the reports I asked for, etc. The sub-agent then returns a GREEN/RED light condition. GREEN means add a summary to changes, commit and proceed. RED means STOP immediately, provide a full overview of the current situation and the sub-agent's findings and wait for the operator's manual review. Then we provide remediation and resume. And so on. 

Managing usage limits is a challenge. I have CODEX/AGY/OpenCode and I use all three. I use Deepseek for architecture/audits/reports, I use a custom model for my art and SOL 5.6 for generic game assets (it makes excellent assets and has great consistency if properly provided with an art styling guide and legit guardrails to work within, and I use AGY for drafting, bouncing ideas, and bulk lightweight work I don't want to soak SOL time into.  

For me it's documentation. Everything is documented. every concept, every instruction, every agent writes a report, every phase is committed with git, every step has a historical record that can be analyzed and debugged making running down issues much faster, and keeping the steps as small as possible helps the agent digest things easier and work within smaller context windows If you permit the agent too much flexibility, it will take the path of least resistance. Every time. All the time.

IDK if this helps... be well, and keep creating. 

This got TLDR, I apologize.

comments.author: Alarming_Turnover578
comments.body:
I usually start with docs, telling ai where should each kind of information go - plans, ai notes, list of game systems, etc.

Then do a few brainstorming and planning sessions, until I and ai have some rough roadmap.

After that I go through the roadmap creating detailed subgoals and steps for current roadmap goal.

Then do separate sessions where AI looks at docs, finds current subgoal and works through steps until current subgoal is finished. With verification and bughunting included.

After each big roadmap goal goes another verification, bughunting, interconnection, optimisation, balance and documentation pass.

Also had problem with docs bloat after some time. I tried several models and they all like to write about what was changed. And they do it everywhere - in roadmap, in changelog, in comments in code, etc. Reorganized my docs a bit and told AI in which file to dump that kind of information and my context is free again.

I also have a tiny INDEX.md file which lists other docs and what is in themsks with a note to only read docs relevant to the current task. As long as your docs are grouped and structured they do not take much space in context. 

Having separate sessions limited in scope to the preplanned goals and systems also helps.

As well as having smaller local model to go through docs and check them for consistency and references to each other.

I also have separate subagents for repeatable tasks like assets manager to keep inventory of requested, available, imported and created assets. Main agent leaves requests on what is needed at future roadmap goals and what is currently needed as well as feedback on current assets. And assets manager acts on them.

For the usage limits I have created simple watchdog tool that agents can use to set limits for their subagent, such as token limit, time limit, steps limit, etc. It detects if any limit is breached and stops subagent, giving info to agent that initiated it.

comments.author: Afterlight_Games
comments.body:
I’ve been building my first Steam game in Godot using ChatGPT for planning, Cursor for coding, and Tripo for some assets. Biggest thing I’ve learned is to tackle one system at a time and actually test it in-game before moving on.

AI can get individual mechanics working pretty quickly, but getting everything to play nicely together is a whole different challenge lol. I also keep a game vision document so I can give AI context without having to explain the entire project every time.

Still figuring out the best workflow myself, but avoiding massive prompts that try to change 10 things at once has helped a lot.

comments.author: guitarist91
comments.body: Commit before every prompt, and when a fix goes sideways just git reset and re-ask with what you learned. Asking it to fix its own fix is where most of the limit goes - three rounds in, it's mostly arguing with itself.
